title: Show HN: Mnemolith – AI coding memory that goes stale when your code changes
text:
Hi HN, I'm Anish. I built Mnemolith because the AI coding tools I use (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) either forget my project between sessions, or remember things that quietly stopped being true. Tell the agent "we use Postgres", migrate to MySQL two weeks later, and it keeps building on the old fact.

How it works:

- It's an MCP server, so Claude Code, Cursor and Codex share one memory per project (keyed by the git repo). - When the agent saves a memory, it can link it to the files it depends on. Mnemolith stores each file's git blob hash. If the file's contents change (committed or not), the memory is set aside and flagged for review, so the agent stops relying on it. - A local dashboard shows what the agent remembers, where each memory came from (tool, session, file versions), and its full history. You can confirm a memory is still true, or retire it and say what's true now. - Contradictions are judged by the agent, not by a similarity threshold. In my calibration, "we use Postgres" vs "we migrated to MySQL" only scored 0.30 similarity, so a threshold can't tell a contradiction from an unrelated fact. - Current memories can sync into a managed section of AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md, so they get reviewed in PRs.

Under the hood it runs on an engine I wrote from scratch in Java: a Redis-compatible server with a built-in memory model and an HNSW vector index. Embeddings run locally (all-MiniLM-L6-v2). Everything stays on your machine.

It's early (v0.2.1). There's no team sync yet beyond the AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md files, and it needs Java 11+ (it downloads a private copy if you don't have one).

I'd really like feedback, especially from people running coding agents on real codebases. What does your agent keep getting wrong?

title: Re: How to spot AI science slop...
text:
Reads kinda dumb, weird and painful.

> Note: Some people write the text, then format it with Claude. In my opinion this isn’t AI slop, whereas AI-generated text that’s manually formatted (also very common) would be AI slop.

I hate it when people do this. I had a manager that fed all our stories through Opus 4.x a year ago and they could easily turn from well defined human-readable requirements to a massive mess of every possible error condition and HTTP code.

When you write, you are communicating one human to another. You are organizing your thoughts. The fact that all of us CAN read and write is only a few centuries old. 1,000 years ago, literacy rates were very low (I've never found a good number on this. Most papers claim it was 2% ~ 5%. I think it was probably closer to 10%, and more than just merchants who needed to track inventor. But a lot of those wax tables and old paper has probably all disintegrated).

I have a feeling the author AI-assisted this. I'd rather read something real, grammar mistakes and all. I realize it may matter less and less as more people start adopting the speaking patterns of their favorite models. "That's a great idea..." and "You're absolutely right to push back on that..."

Generative text use to be really painful for me to read. As I use it more in code, I'm getting more use to it, and I'm not sure if I entirely like it, even when it's helpful.

title: One setjmp call was eating 81% of Geolith's emulator frame time
text:
I'm the developer of NeoBox (https://neo-box.app). It's a Neo Geo emulator frontend for Mac + iPhone + iPad as one universal app.

I'm using Rupert Carmichael's amazing Geolith library https://gitlab.com/jgemu/geolith for the actual emulation. I then have a Metal-backed rendering pipeline.

Recent versions where I was porting NeoBox for iPhone and testing on my iPhone 15 Pro, I noticed it getting hot! Granted I've had the phone for a few years, but I was wondering if there were was something I could do about it. Enter Claude...

Started profiling a frame and where time was being most spent, and it turns out that 81% of the frame time was being spent on signal masks. What this mean that a Neo Geo frame was taking 8.5 ms on Apple silicon.

That's all fine and dandy on my MacBook Pro with an M1 Max chip...but definitely was causing heat and battery drain issues on my iPhone. You would figure that most time should be on emulation time and not on two specifically on sigprocmask and sigalstack.

Went deep with Claude and here's what I learned:

- How the CPU is being emulated, it traps errors before touching memory

- Almost 25,000 times per frame!

- The guard was using setjmp, which also saves the signal mask

- But saving the mask was unnecessary, but that's setjmp's default behavior

- There's a variant _setjmp, that SKIPS that signal mask... and thus is WAY faster

- measured on my iPhone: setjmp 281 ns per cal, _setjmp 2.1 ns per call

- That's around 130x improvement

I'm happy to say that the change and improvement has been graciously merged upstream so anyone using Geolith can reap the benefits, not just NeoBox: https://gitlab.com/jgemu/geolith/-/merge_requests/64

I just wanted to share this story as a gentle reminder to give back when you can graciously and without any sense of entitlement. AI can be a force for good should we choose it. Also it's fun to freshen and learn more about OS primitives and syscalls :)

title: Show HN: Ternlux – Free, local-first, bring-your-own-key AI pipeline builder
text:
For the past 12 years as a data engineer, I've been building pipelines across many different business categories and sizes. Most pipelines that I’ve encountered were relatively simple jobs and required more orchestration and infrastructure than the work seems to justify. I wanted to make it easier for business users or analysts to take on the less complicated requests and technical engineers be able to focus on more complex pipelines. So in the past year I've been building a local desktop application (Mac/PC/Linux) to make it easy enough for analysts to build pipelines and answer analytical questions they have about their data, no matter their level of technical expertise. It’s called Ternlux, and it streamlines the process of transforming and getting your data where it needs to go.

There are two key features:

- Ask questions: AI helps to write the query for your connection and answer your question - Build reusable workflows: The AI generates SQL, Python, and workflow logic that executes based on your defined rules and triggers

One of the key advantages of the application is you can perform cross-database joins between databases, local files, vector databases, and cloud storage. You describe the workflow you want and the app writes the code and builds the environment to execute it in (for local joins, it uses either JS, Python, or DuckDB to execute the code). For example, if I want to build a workflow that joins a Postgres table with a CSV file and write the results to Snowflake, I just describe the tables I want to use, the keys to join on, and where the join should run. The app takes care of the rest.

I also wanted the app to be as secure as possible. It always asks for approval before performing any database or local file manipulation. It never sends anything to Ternlux servers if you haven’t opted into telemetry. It’s important to note that the app will send query results to your selected AI provider to analyze and answer your questions. It will also send the schema and a small sample size of your data to build workflows properly.

It is a bring your own key application. It supports Gemini, Claude, OpenAI, and any models that are OpenAI compatible (Ollama, LM Studio, Openrouter…). All of your credentials stay encrypted locally. And the app is completely free including all features (besides the AI models you use with your own key obviously).

I’ve built a quick demo showcasing the applications

Demo: https://www.ternlux.com/online-demo/

3-min overview: https://youtu.be/tA7N7wiLliA

The list of connectors that exist: Postgres, MySQL, SQL Server, BigQuery, Snowflake, MongoDB, Pinecone, LanceDB, S3, GCS, Azure Blob, Google Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox, and Google Sheets.

I would love your honest feedback on this.

How can this product be improved?

Would you currently use it as a tool to replace your current tool or in conjunction with your other tools?

What feature do you find most useful and I should focus on from the list?

title: Re: A sci-fi team of artificial contributors for Radic...
text:
Hey everyone! I've open-sourced radicle-team, a project I've been working on for the last couple of months: https://radicle.network/nodes/index.radicle.garden/rad%3Az32... and https://github.com/ales-tsurko/radicle-team

It's a team of sci-fi characters living and working as artificial contributors on Radicle (https://radicle.network). Each character has different skills, a voice and all the characters share a common story. You can configure different models for each one and they work on a pre-configuration basis: you should not worry (or forget) to switch models for different tasks, you can assign a special character with suitable skill set. The expertise is just a way of communication within the team, so you could better understand, which model to choose for a particular task. For example, there is Nico, a junior dev, who could be driven by a fast model like DeepSeek. Or there is Nora, front-end dev, who can use an Anthropic model under the hood.

They are like normal developers, "artificial contributors". You can assign them tasks, they can work on patches, create issues, review patches, and there is an option to configure IRC chat for quick team communication.

Chatting and commenting don't interrupt them from coding, they are independent processes. And they work on a single task at a time - there is a task queue. Tasks can be prioritized. They are sandboxed and you can configure what they can do. All works through the normal Radicle interface, like you would collaborate with normal contributors: patches, issues, labels and mentions.

Right now it uses Claude Code (for Claude) and OpenCode (for other models) under the hood. But I'm considering developing a native harness.

The project is under development and I don't recommend using it for projects in production yet.
